The spec exists because sessions are disposable and big work isn't. Anything that takes more than one
of effort needs a home outside the

, whether that's a file in the repo, a GitHub issue, or an issue tracker the agent can reach. The spec is that home: the goal, the constraints, the decisions made so far, and the list of tickets with their status. Any fresh session can read it and know where the work stands without inheriting the previous session's accumulated noise.
Specs come in recognisable styles, mostly inherited from how teams already write things down. A
(PRD) leans toward the user-facing what and why — features, behaviour, acceptance criteria. A
leans technical — the chosen approach, the alternatives rejected, the trade-offs. At the small end, a plain
with a checklist of tickets does the same job for a multi-session feature. The style matters less than the role: for the
, each of these is the same thing — the durable statement of intent it reads at the start of every session.
